articles.title: What Is Cozanet?
articles.description: A factual introduction to Cozanet: what the company builds, what is live today, what is in development, and what is only planned.
articles.html:
Cozanet is a software infrastructure company building intelligent infrastructure for the digital economy. Its current flagship product, AEGIS, is a financial operating system focused on smart routing between digital assets and financial infrastructure — moving money across Africa's crypto, bank, and mobile money rails.

The brand hierarchy

Cozanet is the company. AEGIS is one product of that company. CZN is the ecosystem token, issued on BNB Smart Chain. The founder is Ifeanyi, known publicly as CozyCrypto. Keeping these four identities distinct matters: when you read about “AEGIS smart routing,” that is a product capability of AEGIS; when you read about Cozanet's developer platform, that is company-level infrastructure that other products will use.

What actually exists today

Cozanet deliberately separates what is live from what is planned. Today, AEGIS is live at aegis.cozanet.net with Phase One: custodial wallets on BNB Smart Chain, token swaps (PancakeSwap routing plus a dedicated CZN/WBNB pool), a treasury fee ledger with on-chain fee collection, in-app and email notifications, and the Cozanet AI assistant with persistent memory. The company website, documentation, roadmap, and changelog are live at cozanet.net.

What is in development

The multi-rail Smart Router — the layer that routes transfers through banking rails, mobile money, Stellar, and Circle Arc/USDC settlement — is in active development and is not yet live. An Android application has been built and is in on-device testing. A developer SDK is being written.

What is planned

CZN fee discounts, platform rewards, and governance mechanics are design goals, not current functionality. A non-custodial wallet option is planned alongside the custodial default, and will not ship without a published migration plan that protects existing wallets.

An honesty policy, in public

Cozanet does not publish user counts, transaction volumes, funding, partnerships, or exchange listings that it cannot verify. Where information is unknown, the company's own pages say so. The roadmap and changelog carry the real record — and if a claim cannot be sourced, it does not appear. That is the standard this site holds itself to.

articles.title: What Is AEGIS and How Does Smart Routing Work?
articles.description: AEGIS is Cozanet's financial operating system. This article explains what is live today and how smart routing between crypto, bank, and mobile money rails is designed to work.
articles.html:
AEGIS is Cozanet's financial operating system for connecting Web3 assets with traditional financial and payment infrastructure. The goal: when someone moves money across Africa's crypto, bank, and mobile money rails, AEGIS decides — automatically — which rail is cheapest or fastest for that specific transfer, and routes through it.

What is live today (Phase One)

AEGIS is deployed at aegis.cozanet.net. Today it provides custodial wallets on BNB Smart Chain (users operate wallets through their AEGIS account), token swaps routed through PancakeSwap with a dedicated CZN/WBNB pool for the CZN token, a treasury fee ledger that records on-chain fee collection, notifications, and the Cozanet AI assistant with persistent memory. This is real, usable software — but it is deliberately called Phase One, because the routing layer it is building toward is not finished.

How smart routing is designed to work

Today, moving money between rails is manual: a person decides to use a bank transfer, a mobile-money provider, or a crypto transfer, and pays whatever that rail costs. The Smart Router inverts this. A transfer request specifies what to move and where; the router queries the available rails (banking, mobile money, blockchain networks such as BNB Smart Chain and Stellar, stablecoin settlement such as Circle Arc/USDC), compares cost, speed, and reliability at that moment, and executes through the best option — with failover to another rail if one fails mid-route.

Why an engine architecture

Routing decisions need current data: rates, rail availability, fees, risk. AEGIS implements this as gateway-first microservices — independent engines (rates, market, risk, treasury, swap, transfer) behind a unified gateway. Each engine owns its domain and scales independently. The frontend holds no business logic; it calls the gateway. This is also what makes the router auditable: every routing decision can be logged with its inputs.

Status: in development

The Smart Router itself is not live. Phase One proves the components — wallets, swaps, fee handling, engine communication — on one rail (BNB Smart Chain). The router that combines multiple rails is the next phase of work. Read the roadmap for the current status of every component.

articles.title: Why Cross-Border Settlement Is Difficult in African Markets
articles.description: Fragmented rails, expensive remittances, currency volatility, and infrastructure gaps: the real reasons cross-border settlement across African markets is hard.
articles.html:
Cross-border settlement in Africa is difficult for structural reasons, not because any single provider is bad at its job. Understanding those reasons explains why Cozanet is building a routing layer rather than another single-rail service.

Fragmented rails

A transfer that crosses an African border usually changes rails at least once: a bank transfer in one country, a mobile-money wallet in another, cash pickup somewhere in between. Each rail has its own settlement times, fees, operating hours, and failure modes — and each hand-off is a point where cost, delay, or failure is introduced. There is no single network that spans the continent's payments the way, for example, card networks span consumer payments globally.

Remittances remain expensive

World Bank remittance price data has consistently shown that sending money to Sub-Saharan Africa costs more than the global average — historically in the range of high single-digit percentages of the amount sent, versus a global average of roughly half that. On small transfers, fixed fees can consume a large share of the value. This is the problem AEGIS's smart-routing design targets directly: when the router can compare rails at transfer time, pricing pressure is applied where it matters — per transfer, not per marketing campaign.

Many currencies, constant conversion

The continent has 50+ national currencies, many of them volatile, and most cross-border transfers require at least one conversion. Conversion spread is a second, less visible fee on top of transfer fees. Stablecoin settlement (the reason AEGIS is building Circle Arc/USDC and Stellar support) is one mechanism for reducing conversion hops — but only where regulation and liquidity allow, which varies by market.

Infrastructure gaps cut both ways

Banking penetration varies widely; mobile money is often the dominant rail; internet and electricity reliability vary by region. Any settlement system that assumes a single rail is available everywhere will fail somewhere it is needed. This is why failover — routing a transfer to an alternate rail when the primary one is down — is a first-class design goal for AEGIS rather than an afterthought.

What AEGIS does about it today

Honestly: not the multi-rail routing yet — that is in development. What is live is Phase One: wallets and swaps on BNB Smart Chain, plus the engine architecture the router needs. The rest of this problem is being built deliberately, one verified component at a time.

articles.title: Cozanet's Approach to Web3-to-Financial Infrastructure
articles.description: How Cozanet connects Web3 assets to traditional financial rails: custodial wallets today, a multi-rail Smart Router in development, and an architecture built for verification.
articles.html:
Most Web3 projects stop at the blockchain. Most fintech projects stop at the bank. Cozanet's premise is that value moving across Africa's economy has to cross both — and that the crossing needs to be automatic.

Start with what Web3 actually offers here

Public blockchains give settlement that is final, fast, and does not require the sender and receiver to share a bank. On BNB Smart Chain, AEGIS already uses this: Phase One wallets hold and swap assets (BNB, USDT, CZN and other BEP-20 tokens), and settlement happens on-chain in seconds to minutes rather than days. Stablecoins add a second property: a value that doesn't require trusting any single national currency.

The honest limitations

Crypto rails alone don't reach most people's money. Bank accounts and mobile-money wallets are where salaries, savings, and daily payments actually live. The last mile of African finance is not a wallet address — and any system that only speaks blockchain cannot serve it. That boundary is exactly what the Smart Router is designed to cross: crypto for cheap, fast settlement where it fits; banking and mobile-money rails for reach where it doesn't.

Architecture: separation of powers

AEGIS is built as gateway-first microservices: a unified gateway handling authentication and rate limiting, and isolated engines behind it — wallet vault, swap, transfer, treasury, rates, market, risk, identity, notifications. Web3 components are engines like any other rail: the system calls them, records what they did, and can route around them. Authentication uses Firebase Auth; data lives in Supabase; both are deliberate production choices, documented rather than hidden.

Custodial today, by design — with a path forward

Phase One wallets are custodial: keys are derived deterministically from a protected master seed and managed server-side, and users operate their wallets through their AEGIS account. This was a deliberate choice for Phase One operability and supportability. It is stated plainly on the security page, with its risks, because pretending it isn't custodial would be worse than being custodial. A non-custodial option is planned — but only with a published migration plan that never orphans an existing wallet.

Verification over marketing

Every public claim Cozanet makes is either live, in development, or planned — and labeled as such. The CZN token page lists contract facts read directly from the chain and says plainly that there are no exchange listings and that fee discounts are planned, not implemented. That discipline is the approach: build the bridge one verified span at a time.

articles.title: Building AEGIS: Architecture, Wallets and Roadmap
articles.description: An engineering view of AEGIS: gateway-first microservices, custodial wallet derivation, audit logging, and a roadmap separated into live, in-development, and planned.
articles.html:
AEGIS is built the way infrastructure should be: boring components, clear contracts between them, and a roadmap that distinguishes what exists from what is being built. This is the engineering view.

Architecture

AEGIS is a gateway-first microservices system. One gateway handles authentication, rate limiting, and routing. Behind it, each functional domain runs as an isolated engine: wallet vault, swap, treasury, transfer, identity, notifications, rates, market, risk, compliance, and the AI orchestrator that routes user intent to specialized reasoning engines. Clients — web and Android — hold no business logic; they call the gateway. Production identity is Firebase Authentication; production data is Supabase. These were deliberate choices, documented in the architecture, not accidents to be reversed.

Wallets

Phase One wallets are custodial. Wallet addresses are derived deterministically — the same account always maps to the same address, and addresses are treated as immutable: they are never re-derived into different addresses or overwritten. Keys are managed server-side; users operate their wallets through their AEGIS accounts (sign-in via email or Google). Transaction construction and signing happen server-side, and broadcasts go to BNB Smart Chain. Swaps route through PancakeSwap, with a dedicated CZN/WBNB pair contract for the CZN token. The design rule that governs all of this: nothing may orphan an existing user's wallet. Any change to wallet architecture requires a published migration plan first.

Audit and stability discipline

Platform events are written to append-only audit logging. Deployment is serverless (Vercel) with CI producing Android builds. The project runs with an explicit stability rule: crashes are fixed first, then broken pages, then UI, then features — and before any change that touches users, the question is asked: will this affect existing production users? If yes, the change ships with an inspection, a blast radius estimate, and a rollback plan.

Roadmap, honestly labeled

Live: wallets, swaps, treasury fee ledger, notifications, AI assistant, this website and docs. In development: the multi-rail Smart Router (banking, mobile money, Stellar, Circle Arc/USDC), the Android app (built; Play Store release pending), the developer SDK. Planned: CZN fee discounts, rewards, governance; a non-custodial wallet option; more rails and coverage. Dates are not published until features ship — the changelog is the record of what is real.
